question_en: Daily price limits are most likely a feature of:
explanation_en: Futures price limits Price limits Define range of permissible prices for a trading session Trading range Upper/lower bounds based on previous day's settlement price Locked limit Trading stops since investors are unwilling to trade at prices within range Expanded limits Limits increased if market is locked limit at close of trading session Daily price limits are a feature of many futures contracts. During a trading session, futures trades can be executed only within those limits, which create a range of acceptable prices. The upper and lower bounds of permissible trade prices are expressed as a given price difference above and below the previous trading session's settlement price. Price limits are imposed to help the clearinghouse manage the credit risk of futures trading. Although the clearinghouse guarantees performance on futures contracts, it is exposed to defaults by traders. The clearinghouse manages this counterparty risk partly by requiring cash margins from traders with futures positions. Price limits constrain the range of possible price changes, thus reducing the potential losses suffered by traders on the wrong side of the market and, as a result, the clearinghouse itself. (Choices A and C) Neither swaps nor forward contract prices are subject to price limits since they are traded in the over-the-counter market. This market has no central location for trading or continuous reporting of trades, so price limits would be difficult to enforce.

option_b: a one-time premium for the right to benefit from an increase in a bond's credit spread.
option_c: the interest, principal, and appreciation on a specific bond in return for a fixed or variable
explanation_en: A European put option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at the exercise price on the date of the option's expiration. If the market price is less than the exercise price, then the put buyer has the right to sell the underlying asset at a higher price than the existing market price. The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the put buyer's payoff. If the market price is not lower than the exercise price, then the put buyer will not exercise the option, and there is no payoff. Therefore, the put buyer's payoff is the greater of (exercise price – market price) and zero. In this scenario, the put's exercise price at expiration is GBP 76, and the value of the underlying is GBP 83. The payoff is the greater of (76 – 83) = GBP −7 and zero, so the payoff is GBP 0. (Choice A) GBP −3 is the put buyer's profit, which equals the payoff minus the amount paid to purchase the option: (0 – 3) = GBP −3. (Choice C) GBP 7 is the result of subtracting the exercise price from the value of the underlying asset.

explanation_en: Interest rate swaps are forward commitment derivatives in which counterparties exchange periodic payment streams based on interest rates. In a fixed-for-floating swap (eg, plain vanilla), one party pays a fixed interest rate on a notional principal amount based on a given currency, while the counterparty pays a floating rate calculated on the same notional principal amount and currency. Payments are made at pre-established dates during the swap's life. With plain vanilla swaps, it is common that each party owes a different amount on each payment date, so by convention the payments are netted and the party with the greater obligation pays the difference between the two payments. This difference between the two payments for the period is the cash due. (Choice B) Credit default swaps require only the credit protection buyer to make periodic payments over the life of the swap. The credit protection seller pays only if there is a default event. (Choice C) In a forward rate agreement (FRA), a single payment is made by one party to the other when the FRA matures.

option_b: negotiate the quantity of the underlying asset.

explanation_en: The maximum gain for option sellers (ie, shorts) is limited to the option premium from the option sale and occurs when the option is out of the money. In such cases, put holders will not exercise their right to sell since the underlying could be sold at the higher market price. If the option is in the money, put holders will exercise their right to sell the asset at the higher strike price, and the short put is obligated to buy the asset at the higher price. The short put's loss at exercise is the difference between the strike price and the market price, and if that difference is greater than the premium received when the option was sold, the seller has a net loss. As the underlying asset price decreases, the put seller faces increasing losses. However, since underlying asset prices cannot fall below zero, the maximum loss is limited. (Choice B) Short calls have limited gains and unlimited losses. Call sellers' gains are limited to the premium received. Potential losses are unlimited since losses increase as underlying asset prices increase, with no theoretical limit. (Choice C) No asset or derivative has unlimited potential gains and losses. Short option maximum gains are always limited.

explanation_en: Derivative contract comparison Forward commitments Contingent claims Contract Exchange of obligations Conveyance of rights Buyer has the right, but no obligation, to exercise; seller's Counterparties Both obligated to perform obligation is contingent on exercise Cost at Usually no cost to either party Buyer pays premium to seller initiation Examples Futures, forwards, most swaps Options, credit default swaps, total return swaps Contingent claims are derivatives that give holders the right to trade the underlying asset at a specified price at a future date. Contract holders do not have to exercise that right, but if they do the original contract seller is obligated to take the other side of the trade that results from the exercise. For a contingent claim, sellers must fulfill their obligations contingent on the contract holders exercising their rights. Contingent refers to the counterparties exchanging a right for an obligation. This is unlike forward commitments, in which both buyers and sellers exchange obligations that each must fulfill. (Choice A) Contingent claim sellers receive a premium for granting contract buyers specified rights. (Choice C) Counterparty credit risk is the uncertainty that a counterparty will fulfill its obligation under a derivative contract. question_en: If a put option holder exercises the option, the original put option seller:
option_a: is obligated to sell the underlying asset.
option_b: is obligated to buy the underlying asset.
option_c: has the right to buy the underlying asset.
explanation_en: Call options are derivatives that give: buyers (ie, long position) the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at the exercise (ie, strike) price and sellers (ie, short position) the obligation to sell the underlying asset at the exercise price if the call buyer decides to exercise the right to buy. Options have asymmetric payoff profiles. The greater the underlying price increase above the exercise price, the greater the gain to the call buyer and loss to the call seller. In contrast, if the underlying price is at or below the exercise price (ie, the option is at the money or out of the money), the call buyer will not exercise and the option's value is zero. No matter how far below the exercise price the asset's value is, the buyer's loss is limited to the original cost of buying the option. Since the most the call buyer can lose is the premium paid, the maximum profit to the call seller is the premium received. (Choice A) The call option seller's potential loss is unlimited since there is theoretically no limit to the underlying asset's appreciation. (Choice C) The put option seller's maximum loss is the option strike price less the premium received.

explanation_en: Credit risk–minimizing features of futures trading Purpose Clearinghouse guarantees Make good on losses of defaulting traders Margin deposits Used to pay for losses day by day Daily price limits Limit traders' losses to insulate clearinghouse Since futures trade only on exchanges, they expose traders to less default risk than over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives such as forwards. question_en: Which of the following best describes the maximum potential gains and losses on a short put at expiration?
explanation_en: Options are derivatives that: give put buyers the right but not the obligation to sell the underlying asset at the exercise (ie, strike) price or give put sellers the obligation to buy the underlying asset at the exercise price if a put buyer decides to exercise the right to sell. Options have asymmetric payoff profiles. At any underlying price equal to or greater than the exercise price (ie, at or out of the money (T63457)), the put buyer does not exercise, and the option's value is zero. If the option expires unexercised, the seller's profit is the premium received from selling the option. The further the underlying price falls below the exercise price, the greater the gain for the put buyer and the greater the loss for the seller. A put seller incurs the maximum loss when the underlying price drops to zero: the strike price paid for a worthless asset (ie, option exercise value (D1411)) less the premium received at the initial sale. (Choice A) A call option seller's potential loss is unlimited since, theoretically, the underlying asset has the potential for unlimited appreciation. (Choice B) The strike price is a put's maximum value. A put seller's maximum loss is this amount minus the premium.

explanation_en: A fixed-for-floating interest rate swap (ie, plain vanilla swap) is an over-the-counter derivative contract in which two parties agree to exchange periodic cash flows based on an agreed rate and notional principal. One party pays a fixed rate while the other party pays a floating (variable) rate (eg, LIBOR) in return. In this case, the company has a floating-rate loan with a bank. It can agree to a plain vanilla swap with a notional principal equal to the loan principal and pay a fixed rate to the swap counterparty. In return, the counterparty pays the floating rate to the company, which the company uses to pay the loan's floating rate to the bank. The company has effectively converted its loan from a floating rate to a fixed rate. The fixed rate the company pays in the swap may be higher than the floating rate but may be preferable to eliminate the uncertainty of the floating-rate payments. (Choices A) A total return swap is a credit derivative in which one party agrees to periodically pay the net of principal, interest, and changes in value on a bond in return for regular payments from a second party. If the bond defaults, the second party's payments continue while the first party's payments decrease substantially or go to zero. (Choice C) In a credit default swap, one party makes a series of payments to another party in return for an agreed payment when a credit event (eg, default) occurs. This arrangement is a form of credit protection analogous to insurance, not an exchange of floating-rate payments for fixed- rate payments.

question_en: For a trader with no positions in the underlying asset or related options, the maximum gain on a short call is best described as:
option_c: the strike price less the premium received.
explanation_en: Initiating futures positions requires traders to meet an initial margin requirement in cash, which ensures that a trader has enough funds on hand to cover any losses. This is essential since futures settle daily, and therefore losses must be paid for immediately after every trading session. Futures margins are described as performance bonds or good faith deposits. To ensure that there are adequate funds to cover losses, the margin account balance must be maintained above a minimum amount known as the maintenance margin, which is usually lower than the initial margin requirement. If the account balance falls below the maintenance margin, there is a demand (ie, margin call) for additional funds. The amount of the call is equal to the amount of cash necessary to raise the account balance to the initial margin requirement, not the maintenance margin. Failure to meet the call in full can result in liquidation of under-margined positions. (Choice A) The money to buy the underlying asset is required only at expiration and only if the long decides to buy the underlying asset at that time. Most futures positions are liquidated prior to expiration. (Choice C) The money required to return the account balance (ie, equity) to the maintenance margin would be correct if this were a securities account margin call, instead of a futures margin call.
